ai.title: Mixed Affective Episode
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: A mixed affective episode features simultaneous manic and depressive symptoms. Recognising it guides urgent management and prevents misdiagnosis as pure mania or depression.

b: Higher risk of suicide and rapid cycling
sections.p: In bipolar disorder, a mixed affective episode occurs when criteria for both mania/hypomania and major depression are met concurrently or in rapid alternation within a week.

t.b: Does the patient meet full criteria for mania/hypomania plus ≥3 depressive symptoms? – Confirms mixed episode
Are depressive symptoms present for at least half the duration of the manic episode? – Aligns with local diagnostic practice

b: Manic symptoms: pressured speech, decreased need for sleep, psychomotor agitation, risky behaviour
Depressive symptoms: anhedonia, weight change, psychomotor retardation, suicidal ideation
sections.p: Mixed episodes blend elevated energy, irritability, and depressive features such as hopelessness, guilt, or suicidal thoughts. They are not simply irritability in mania.

t.b: Is the manic severity moderate‑severe? – Helps gauge urgency of mood stabiliser
Is depressive severity moderate‑severe? – Indicates need for antidepressant‑sparing strategy

sections.p: Mixed episodes carry the highest short‑term mortality in bipolar disorder, often presenting with agitation, insomnia, and suicidal behaviour, requiring rapid stabilisation.

t.a: Suicidal risk assessment tool (e.g., Columbia Scale)
t.b: Is the patient at imminent risk? – Determines need for admission or close observation

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, electrolytes, LFT, renal, TSH)
t.b: Are there medical contributors or contraindications to lithium/valproate? – Guides safe drug choice

b: Identify at least three manic and three depressive symptoms occurring together
Explain why antidepressants alone are contraindicated
sections.p: Examiners test ability to differentiate mixed episodes from pure mania, depression, or psychosis and to choose appropriate acute management.

t.b: Is lithium therapeutic and safe? – Guides dose adjustment if available
Are there conduction abnormalities? – Avoids valproate in hepatic or cardiac compromise

b: Confusing agitation from mixed state with psychosis alone
sections.p: Students often label irritability as pure mania or treat with antidepressants, worsening agitation and suicide risk.

t.a: If lithium unavailable, use valproate or carbamazepine
t.b: What alternative stabiliser can be given? – Provides fallback in low‑resource settings

t.a: If no serum level testing, monitor for tremor, polyuria, and renal function
t.b: How to ensure safety without labs? – Emphasises clinical monitoring
